access.edition_or_version: Penguin Classics, trans. Leonard M. Tancock (UK 1981; US 1982); original 1665; public-domain English text at Project Gutenberg #9105

mechanics.premise: Several hundred short maxims re-describing admired human motives — virtue, friendship, love, loyalty, generosity — as refined operations of self-love and self-esteem.
mechanics.point_of_view: Impersonal gnomic observer with no character and no plot; authority carried entirely by compression and antithesis.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Antithesis; balanced parallel clauses; occasional self-qualifying hedges that scope a generalization; the portable one-sentence unit as the form of the insight.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Recognition -> deflation -> self-implication: the reader catches the attributed motive in their own case before the sentence finishes.
mechanics.conventions: French classical moralist tradition (with Pascal and La Brouyere); the model from which the literary maxim and the modern 'cynical' sensibility take their shape.
tone_mechanisms: echoic recall of a shared ideal
mechanics.critical_reception: First published 1665 and expanded by the author across editions; described in reference accounts as portraying human conduct with a cynical attitude toward professed virtue and declarations of affection.
mechanics.verification_note: Existence, 1665 first publication, authorship, and cynical characterization confirmed via Wikipedia API extract (Francois de La Rochefoucauld) on 2026-09-24; edition metadata via publisher catalog. Analysis covers the collection's method as documented; no maxim reproduced verbatim in this silo.
